[COMPANY_B] did not bill clients for work [PERSON_A] performed independently, which included elevation surveys. [PERSON_C] was one of the owners of [COMPANY_A], a company that sold medical equipment for use by elderly people and people with disabilities. Around September 2006, [PERSON_C] contacted [COMPANY_B] about surveying a property [COMPANY_A] had purchased in [LOCATION_A]. [COMPANY_B] sent [PERSON_A] to speak with [PERSON_C] about that property. After [PERSON_A] began work there, [PERSON_C] asked him to perform an elevation survey and complete an elevation certificate for property in [LOCATION_B]. [PERSON_A] made two trips to the [LOCATION_B] property and worked approximately 10 to 15 hours on the survey. He used his own surveying equipment and did not drive a company vehicle. On the elevation certificate, he listed his title as “Land Surveyor,” left “Company Name” blank, and listed his home address. He gave [PERSON_C] a handwritten invoice that listed his personal address and did not refer to [COMPANY_B]. [COMPANY_B] did not issue an invoice for [PERSON_A]’s work at the [LOCATION_B] property and was not paid for that project. Twenty days after [PERSON_A] completed the elevation certificate, [PERSON_C] signed a check dated November 1, 2006, from [COMPANY_C] payable to [PERSON_A] for [CURRENCY_AMOUNT_A]. [PERSON_A] testified that he thought the check paid for his work at the [LOCATION_B] property but could not confirm that, while [PERSON_C] testified that he did not know what the check paid for. After completing the work, [PERSON_A] realized that he had made a 30.48-meter error on the flood-elevation certificate: he recorded a base flood elevation of approximately 180.75 meters instead of approximately 211.84 meters for Buildings 1 through 5. [PERSON_C] alleges that this error caused the certificates to incorrectly state that the [LOCATION_B] property was outside the 100-year flood plain. [PERSON_B] testified that [PERSON_A] was acting independently when he worked on the [LOCATION_B] property, that the work was not a project of [COMPANY_B], that [COMPANY_B] was not paid for it, that [COMPANY_B] did not send [PERSON_C] or [COMPANY_A] an invoice for it, and that [PERSON_B] did not know about the work until months later, when [PERSON_A] spoke with him about the error.

neutral_en: [PERSON_A] and [PERSON_B] were married. [PERSON_A] had breathing ailments, including aggravation of preexisting asthma and hypersensitivity pneumonitis. [PERSON_A] and [PERSON_B] alleged that [PERSON_A]'s breathing ailments were caused by exposure to [PRODUCT_A] and [PRODUCT_B]. [PERSON_A] and [PERSON_B] alleged that [PRODUCT_A] and [PRODUCT_B] came from [PRODUCT_C] used by [COMPANY_D], and that [COMPANY_A], [COMPANY_B], and [COMPANY_C] manufactured those paints. [PERSON_A] was formerly employed by [COMPANY_D]. [PERSON_C] testified that he did not know how often [PERSON_A] was in the Exterior Finish Booth, how close [PERSON_A] was to the Prime Booth or paint sprayers, what ventilation equipment was used, or the frequency and level of [PERSON_A]'s exposure. [PERSON_C] based his causation testimony on [PERSON_A]'s general statement that he was in and out of the area regularly. [PERSON_C] reviewed only one pulmonary function test and did not review [PERSON_A]'s other medical records for the relevant period. [PERSON_C] testified that [PERSON_A]'s current respiratory problems could have been an aggravation of preexisting asthma that existed before [PERSON_A]'s employment by [COMPANY_D], exacerbated by nonspecific irritants regardless of exposure at [COMPANY_D] to the chemicals at issue. [PERSON_C] identified three potential causes for [PERSON_A]'s alleged aggravation of preexisting asthma: exposure to [PRODUCT_B], exposure to [PRODUCT_A], or chronic exposure to unidentified nonspecific irritants. [PERSON_D] testified that heating materials coated with activated polyurethane and epoxy resin products, including heating from welding, produces decomposition products that can include components of the paints, phthalic acid anhydride and similar anhydrides, and isocyanate monomers. [COMPANY_A], [COMPANY_B], and [COMPANY_C] disputed that [PERSON_D]'s affidavit established that [PERSON_A] was actually exposed to [PRODUCT_A] or [PRODUCT_B], or that such exposure caused [PERSON_A]'s breathing problems.

The physician reported that [PERSON_A] could return to work on February 19, 2000, with limitations: [PERSON_A] could not lift anything heavier than 6.8 kilograms and could walk only four hours per day. On February 25, 2000, two of [PERSON_A]'s superiors met with [PERSON_A] and told [PERSON_A] that [PERSON_A] had one "last chance" to improve [PERSON_A]'s attendance. The blood and alcohol testing occurred on February 17, 2000, involved the use of a needle to extract blood from [PERSON_A], and required [PERSON_A] to provide a urine sample.

neutral_en: [COMPANY_A] filled approximately 50-kilogram rice sacks, stacked 36 to 42 sacks on each pallet in cross-tied layers, and applied glue between the layers. The pallets were shipped one layer high and strapped to trucks, but a warehouse operator stacked them three pallets high after unloading. On November 3, 1994, sacks had fallen in the warehouse, and [PERSON_A], a longshore worker, was assigned to collect them. While [PERSON_A] was picking up sacks with his back to the stack, two pallets collapsed and completely covered him. [PERSON_A] was taken to a hospital and later underwent surgery for a hernia and for cervical discs at two levels; the cervical fusions failed, and thoracic outlet syndrome was also diagnosed. [PERSON_A] did not return to work and continued to have lower-back and right-knee pain. The parties disputed whether the mill's original stacking and gluing or the warehouse's three-high stacking contributed to the collapse.

[PERSON_A]가 등을 돌린 채 떨어진 포대를 줍던 중 팔레트 두 개가 무너져 포대들이 [PERSON_A]를 완전히 덮쳤다. neutral_en: [PERSON_A] purchased [VEHICLE_A] from [COMPANY_A], a used-car dealership that had immediately purchased the vehicle from [COMPANY_B] after a trade-in. Several months after acquiring [VEHICLE_A], [PERSON_A] was involved in an automobile accident. [PERSON_A] suffered severe injuries in the automobile accident. [PERSON_A] alleged that [COMPANY_B] failed to attach a revised airbag warning label to [VEHICLE_A]. [PERSON_A] alleged that the revised airbag warning label would have prevented the injuries suffered in the accident. [COMPANY_B] had previously serviced [VEHICLE_A] regularly. [COMPANY_B] asserted that the existing warning label was not inadequate or defective and that the replacement warning label applied only to vehicles manufactured after 1997, not to [VEHICLE_B]. It was uncontested that the applicable rule did not require manufacturers or dealerships to install revised warning labels in vehicles manufactured before February 1997. [PERSON_A] admitted in the pleadings that, at the time of the accident, the airbags functioned as designed. Both parties conceded that [COMPANY_B] never worked on the airbags.
